full_text:
Former Dolphin Tua Tagovailoa has been named the Falcons' starting quarterback to begin the season. Justin Casterline / Getty Images
The Atlanta Falcons have named Tua Tagovailoa their starting quarterback, ending the NFL’s most protracted quarterback competition at least for now.
Tagovailoa, 28, will be making his 77th regular-season start when the Falcons take on the Steelers in Pittsburgh on Sunday. He came to Atlanta on a one-year contract for the veteran minimum salary ($1.2 million) this offseason after six years in Miami, where he made the Pro Bowl in 2023 but was released two seasons later despite a dead cap hit of nearly $100 million to the Dolphins.
Tagovailoa beat out Michael Penix Jr., the Falcons’ No. 8 pick in 2024, for the starting job, but Penix is still expected to have a chance to overtake Tagovailoa at some point this season. Penix, 26, suffered a torn ACL in Week 11 last year and was only cleared for 11-on-11 practice on Aug. 24.
Coach Kevin Stefanski announced Monday that Penix will be inactive for Week 1, while Cooper Rush will serve as Tagovailoa’s backup in the opener.
“Really, really proud of those guys,” Stefanski said. “Those guys have worked like crazy all offseason, and they have pushed each other and supported each other, and that’s what we’ll continue to do with Tua. We’ll support him and make sure this is a collective group that is constantly looking to help each other.”
Tagovailoa missed the first week of training camp with back spasms and then struggled in the early weeks of practice, but Atlanta’s coaches have been consistently optimistic about his progress.
“As you get through camp, you start to hone in on what each quarterback does well, and you want to devise the offense in terms of how they play and what suits their eye,” offensive coordinator Tommy Rees said, adding of Tagovailoa, “he’s taking a lot of ownership in the operations part of the offense. We’ve asked him to do a lot of stuff he really hasn’t done in his career.”
The decision to go with Tagovailoa will limit Atlanta’s ability to throw the ball downfield because of his relative lack of arm strength compared to Penix. But Tagovailoa has been the much more accurate of the two quarterbacks throughout his career with a 68 percent career completion percentage.
“When things are clean, he’s as accurate as they get,” Rees said.
The Falcons will still be highly incentivized to start Penix at some point this season because he is halfway through his rookie contract, and the team has not decided yet whether to pick up the fifth-year option that would cover the 2028 season.
“(Penix) is getting better and better and better, and I’m very proud of how far he has come,” said Stefanski, who also said he wouldn’t speculate about the Falcons’ QB depth chart beyond Week 1. “I can’t overstate how proud I am of Mike and how he pushes and what he has put his body through. … This will continue to be something where we work together with Mike. We are all on the same page. Everybody feels good about where Mike is headed, and he’ll continue to work like crazy.”

full_text:
Brad Idzik, 34, will call plays for the Panthers this season for the first time as offensive coordinator. Phelan M. Ebenhack / Associated Press
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — Whatever he draws up for the first play against the Chicago Bears on Sunday, it will be hard for Brad Idzik to top his lone call from the 2020 Pro Bowl.
Idzik was in his first year as a low-level offensive assistant with the Seattle Seahawks, whose staff was selected to coach the NFC team after an early exit from the 2019 playoffs. Brian Schottenheimer, the Seahawks offensive coordinator, tasked the 28-year-old Idzik with coming up with a trick play for the game in Orlando, Fla.
Idzik landed on a double pass that tiny Presbyterian College had completed against Wake Forest shortly after Idzik’s playing career with the Demon Deacons ended. So at an NFC offensive meeting, Idzik explained to superstars like Drew Brees, Russell Wilson, Davante Adams and Ezekiel Elliott the play would start with a backward lateral off the artificial turf at Camping World Stadium, with the hope being the defense would assume the play was dead because the ball hit the ground.
“As you can imagine, a mid-20s (coach) standing in front of this group of Pro Bowlers, Drew Brees and all these guys, showing them this Presbyterian (film) cut-up of them throwing the ball down the field,” Idzik recalled. “I’m like, ‘All right, boys, this is what we’re gonna do.’”
Schottenheimer found a spot in the second quarter to try it. Wilson skipped a pass to Adams, who sent a wobbler to Kenny Golladay for a 34-yard completion. A play caller was born.
“You can go back and find it. We ended up throwing the bounce pass for a completion in the Pro Bowl, which I thought was the coolest thing ever,” Idzik said. “That was my first one and it’s like, ‘Hey, all this stuff can work if you design it right and get the right guys doing the right jobs.’”
The Bears’ defense will be playing with a higher intensity than the AFC’s when Idzik debuts as the Carolina Panthers’ play caller. He’s 34 now, no longer the NFL’s youngest offensive coordinator as he was when he was hired in 2024 but still six years younger than Panthers long snapper J.J. Jansen.
Idzik’s youthfulness, and the fact he’s not the head coach, help him connect with quarterback Bryce Young and the Panthers’ other offensive players on a different level than coach Dave Canales, who announced in February he was handing off the play-calling duties .
When Idzik was hired in Seattle, he impressed Canales with his football IQ, work ethic and love for a game he’d grown up with as part of a three-generation NFL family.
“You could feel there was a sense of legacy with him. You could feel there’s a lot of passion with him and he’s shown that,” Canales said. “I can confidently say Brad Idzik is the hardest worker on our staff. I can also say he’s the most conditioned and in shape coach on our staff as well. I’ve been chasing him for 10 years now, trying to keep up with that guy.
“It’s his work ethic. It’s how much he cares about the players, how much he cares about being excellent that gave me the confidence to give him this opportunity.”
Before the Panthers opened the preseason in Canton, Ohio, Idzik visited the Pro Football Hall of Fame’s archives, where he found the bio for his grandfather, John Idzik, in the media guide for the Super Bowl-champion 1970 Baltimore Colts.
After a four-year stretch as the University of Detroit’s head coach, John Idzik had stops as the offensive backfield coach for the Miami Dolphins and Colts before serving as the offensive coordinator for the Philadelphia Eagles and New York Jets. He died in 2013 during Brad Idzik’s senior year at Wake.
“My dad says it all the time,” Brad said. “He’s like, ‘Man, I wish you could have seen him coach. I wish he could have seen you coach.’”
But Idzik had an early exposure to the NFL through his father, also named John, who worked in the front offices for a handful of teams, including a two-year stint as the Jets general manager in 2013-14.
Brad Idzik’s earliest football memories were sweating in the metal bleachers at the old Tampa Stadium when his dad was the Buccaneers’ coordinator of football administration. When his children were old enough, John Idzik would have each of the three join him on separate days at the Bucs’ training camp at the University of Tampa.
“We’d go spend the night and go to the food hall,” Idzik said. “You’d jump in the golf cart with him going from practice to meeting and dropping you back off at the hotel where they’re staying.”
As a middle schooler in Arizona, Idzik would do a mock draft every year of who the Cardinals should select. In 2006, he thought the Cards should take Georgia tight end Leonard Pope. It turns out the Cardinals’ decision-makers also liked Pope, and had decided to take him in the third round. John Idzik, the team’s director of football operations, called his son and let on like he had influenced the pick.
“I said, ‘Now you cannot tell anybody. Nobody knows this. We’re on the clock right now. But we’re gonna pick your guy, Leonard Pope,’” John Idzik said with a laugh.
“He wasn’t just a fly-by-night, pick the Topps card candidates for the draft. He would study guys,” John added. “When I would go to a school or a practice or a game, he’d ask me about guys.”
Idzik’s interest in the draft continued through his years at Wake Forest, where he was a special teams player and reserve receiver after transferring from Lehigh following the second of two ACL surgeries. Idzik and fellow walk-on Jordan Garside would reserve a lecture hall in the business school, write their mocks on the whiteboard and throw a two-person draft party.
“We just ordered pizza and hung out. I don’t think anyone else really shared the interest that him and I did,” Garside said. “It wasn’t like a casual thing for us. We were diving into the players and what their next pick was.”
Even at a school like Wake Forest, Idzik’s academic pursuits stood out. “I think he might have been the only player on the team majoring in mathematical business,” Garside said.
He likely was also the only player who spent his last semester studying abroad at Cambridge. Idzik might have gone into the scouting or business side of football had he not sent an email to Stanford coach David Shaw, who brought him in as a graduate assistant. Idzik was at Stanford for five seasons, leaving with a master’s degree in liberal arts and a familiar career direction, but one of his own choosing.
“I always appreciated that about my dad. He always made sure that I wasn’t doing football because he was in it,” Idzik said. “He wanted me to carve my own path.”
John Idzik, who’s retired and lives in Florida, said he and his wife, Carol, encouraged their children to follow their dreams. Bryant, their older son, is an engineer for SpaceX, while their daughter, Holly, is an elementary school teacher and yoga instructor.
“We’ve got three kids (with) different interests and personalities,” John said. “And as parents, all we wanted is to find your passion, chase your passion and we’ll help you any way we can. And Brad’s just happened to be football.”
Idzik helped Canales prepare for offensive coordinator interviews when both were in Seattle, then accompanied him to Tampa when Canales landed the OC job with the Buccaneers in 2023. Two years later Idzik had his first coordinator gig.
“I remember his first year here, he was always in cleats running around, doing routes and stuff like that. I’m like, ‘That’s our OC? Just running around doing that?’” Panthers tight end Tommy Tremble said. “But he’s a cool cat, man. We’ve got a lot of respect for Brad.”
Idzik’s energetic personality is a nice complement to Young’s even-keeled demeanor, according to offensive pass game coordinator Mike Bercovici.
“The pre-snap communications, getting (Young) hyped after a great play in practice — that’s definitely our culture here is keeping things upbeat and showing appreciation for guys when they do…

full_text:
Bears quarterback Caleb Williams acknowledged the way the team lost the divisional-round playoff game to the Rams "still bothers me." Patrick McDermott / Getty Images
Less than an hour after the Chicago Bears’ 2025 season ended with a crushing 20-17 overtime home loss to the Los Angeles Rams, Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams crossed paths in the hallway between the Bears locker room and the Soldier Field news conference space.
Johnson had just finished answering questions for nine minutes — on the defeat, on the exhilarating season, on the future — and Williams was headed to give his own eulogy.
For a few seconds, though, the coach and quarterback stopped. They spoke to one another, hugged, then held that moment for an extra beat.
This was, in essence, a thank-you note. Genuine and reciprocal.
A few months later, even the oft hard-edged Johnson still felt gratitude for what that short embrace represented. He paused and, through glassy eyes, offered this.
“It’s why you do what you do as a coach. You know?” Johnson told The Athletic . “At this level, yeah, you want to win games and all that. But the relationships you forge, it’s really still all about that.”
Chapter 1 of the Johnson-Williams story didn’t reach the desired destination with the Bears falling three victories short of a Super Bowl triumph. Yet that stage of the pair’s partnership was undeniably a smash success. For the 11 wins, the NFC North title and the playoff victory over Green Bay, no doubt. But also for the bond that strengthened between coach and quarterback. And not just any ol’ coach and quarterback — Johnson and Williams, the two leaders who together will define the direction of the franchise for the next decade.
That’s why the emotion inside that quick hug felt so profound.
“There’s nobody on the team I spent more time with than him,” Johnson said. “In that moment, you’re both disappointed with the result. And yet you’re appreciative of each other.
“It’s just disappointment that it’s ending.”
That heaviness was palpable. But almost immediately, so, too, was the duo’s urge to get back to work. Together.
Now? The ride begins again. Week 1 has arrived. The Bears, after another demanding training camp, are headed to Charlotte for Sunday’s opener against the Carolina Panthers with grand aspirations for what they can achieve this season.
It’s enough to get the wheels turning in multiple directions.
The last meaningful game, that is — to take nothing away from those eight preseason snaps he took against the Bengals last month.
Rewind to Jan. 18 at Soldier Field for the divisional round of the NFC playoffs. Before the hug.
What a night that was by Lake Michigan — full of ambience, emotion and stadium-shaking theatrics as the Bears continued their remarkable season.
We all know the play from that season-ending loss that created the most conversation and received the most offseason airtime. Williams to Cole Kmet. Fourth-and-everything. Final seconds. Touchdown. Pure madness.
To be frank, that play put the entire NFL on notice. What a moment. Especially on that stage, under those circumstances.
The Bears, so many around the league concluded, suddenly had themselves one of those guys: a quarterback magician, a cold-blooded playmaker capable of sprinting 26 yards beyond the line of scrimmage to evade pressure, then possessing the instincts, vision and arm talent to rip a ball 45 yards downfield through the winter chill to tie a playoff game.
Still, a couple of other moments from that January night are worth recounting one last time before the Bears charge into this season. Remember that national anthem, Chicago style, by local legend Jim Cornelison? That felt like something of an arrival for Williams, an awe-filled moment that gave him a true taste of the stage he wants to be on and return to many times throughout his career.
He could see his breath but couldn’t really hear himself think. Chicago’s football passion was lit.
“It was one of the coolest, most surreal, movie-kind of feelings,” Williams said last week during a laid-back conversation inside the X’s and O’s room at Halas Hall. “Just sitting on the sideline, like ‘Wow! I’m here. We’re here. Let’s show up, make some plays and put on for this city.’”
Of course, there is also Williams’ final pass that evening — an unfortunate overtime turnover, with the Bears closing in on a possible walk-off field goal but instead setting the Rams up for their own season-prolonging scoring drive.
Second-and-8 from the Rams’ 48, Williams threw toward receiver DJ Moore. A slight disconnect existed between the quarterback and his intended target. As a result, Rams safety Kam Curl made a diving interception. That was a play with huge ramifications that, to some extent, still sticks with Williams.
“It burns,” he said. “It burns. It’s frustrating. Still.
“It still bothers me today. Every single time that play pops up. Or if the Cole Kmet play pops up, it feels like it was for nothing in a sense.”
Truth be told, the autopsy results on that play proved to be far less juicy than one might imagine, a sort of “it is what it is” collective miscue at the worst possible time.
If Johnson and his coaching staff had to do it over again, they’d probably pull something different from the call sheet, a bread-and-butter concept the offense had more familiarity with and more documented success running.
If rookie receiver Luther Burden III had to do it over again, as the first read on that play, he would have found a cleaner release off the snap and not been engulfed so quickly by cornerback Darious Williams.
If Moore had to do it over again, he’d probably attack his 58th snap of that night and his 1,104th of the season with more purpose and speed. Even with an over route that, under very few scenarios becomes part of the progression, Moore should have stayed full throttle and recognized the leverage in the secondary to flatten his route. At a minimum, he could have worked harder to disrupt Curl’s pick attempt. Worst case: offensive pass interference.
And if Williams had to do it again, he’d probably lock into the game situation, to the time and score, down and distance, and dial back his aggressiveness to move him from his unavailable first read (Burden) to a reliable safety valve option in the right flat (Kmet).
In retrospect, Williams said, he believes that play can be instructive for him, particularly when it comes to his communication process with teammates.
“Yeah,” he said, “just throughout the year, with new plays, old plays, go over every single detail. If something pops in your mind, don’t hold back. Just so that when those moments show up, you’re on the same page with your guys.”
Still, if Curl doesn’t make a clutch diving grab as the ball nosedived toward the grass, that’s merely an incomplete pass that no one remembers.
But that’s football. That’s the thin line between moving on to play for an NFC championship and trudging into the heaviest first stage of the offseason. That’s a margin-for-error lesson, a moment that may continue to burn for a while.
Still, Williams has found appropriate perspective. “You change your lens,” he said, “and you figure out it was meant to be. And that it’s going to do me good and it’s going to do us good in the years to come when we get to those moments again.”
Yes, that embrace we described from last winter was significant. But it was also followed by a spring and summer in which the coach and his QB1 continued to put the pedal down on building their relationship, on sharpening their collective vision for the offense, on drilling down on the details that can take the team to new levels.
Johnson and Williams have arrived at the starting gate for this season in a healthy place.
During the early stages of their first camp together last summer, Williams had his concerns about how his connection with Johnson would evolve. Absolutely flooded with the details and demands of learning a new offense, the Bears quarterback later acknowledged…

full_text:
Expectations are high for Aaron Donald, Kyler Murray and Mike McDaniel in 2026. Illustration: Dan Goldfarb / The Athletic; photos: Ryan Kang/ Getty Images, Mike Coppola / Getty Images, Rich Storry / Imagn Images
It’s finally here: Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season. It’s a time of great hope for fans — because no matter how a team may look on paper, circumstances can change quickly once teams take the game field.
With that in mind, we asked The Athletic ’s NFL writers to think big, have some fun and make one bold prediction for each of the league’s 32 teams.
It’s safe to say Harrison’s NFL introduction has not gone as planned. Labeled as a generational talent before the 2024 draft, the wide receiver put up decent numbers as a rookie but struggled to make contested catches. Last season he battled injuries. Year 3 should bring a jump. Harrison has a solid comfort level with QB Jacoby Brissett. And he knows he has a lot to prove. This doesn’t mean Harrison will be among the NFL’s top receivers (the Cardinals have additional threats in Trey McBride, Michael Wilson and Jeremiyah Love), but he should start to resemble the playmaker everyone expected. — Doug Haller
Just predicting Robinson to break the yards-from-scrimmage mark wouldn’t be all that bold. He came within 211 yards of Chris Johnson’s record (2,509 yards in 2009) last year. To set the all-purpose mark (which includes return yards), he’ll need to top Darren Sproles’ 2,696 in 2011. This is not a bet that Robinson will return kicks for the Falcons this year. It’s a bet he’ll be overfed in both the rushing and passing scheme in Atlanta. — Josh Kendall
The arrival of Jesse Minter as head coach and Anthony Weaver as defensive coordinator has coincided with the return of swagger and confidence to a defense that fell on hard times last year. The addition of Trey Hendrickson and return of Nnamdi Madubuike has surely helped, too. Minter has brought in a defensive system that both attacks and deceives. The Ravens will need bounce-back years from Roquan Smith and Marlon Humphrey, but the mix of accomplished veterans and talented young players, plus a more attacking mindset, is a good recipe for the return of the ball-hawking Baltimore defense from the past. — Jeff Zrebiec
Walker was a fourth-round pick just a year ago, and those who have worked closely with him insist he’s on the verge of greatness . The gargantuan nose tackle slid down the 2025 draft chutes over a nagging back problem the University of Kentucky declined to shut down. So Walker soldiered forth, competing the best he could despite lost-cause game situations. Those performances hurt his stock. Buffalo weighed those reports before adding Walker and molding the rookie to become a star prospect who started every game except the opener. Walker is a 6-foot-7, 331-pound mauler, his oversized frame propelled by a relentless engine. Walker will see recurring opportunities to annihilate offensive lines and leave carriers in a heap. Those visuals will go a long way in establishing him as a bona fide baddie. — Tim Graham
The Panthers’ defense was the NFL’s worst in 2024, when Carolina gave up 404.5 yards and 31.4 points a game, and became the fourth team in NFL history to allow 3,000 rushing yards. Derrick Brown’s return helped the Panthers climb back to respectability last season (16th in total defense). And they look poised to take another jump this year, following the additions of edge rusher Jaelan Phillips and linebackers Devin Lloyd and Bobby Okereke. The interior D-line depth is a little lean, but the back end should be in good shape, provided Mike Jackson repeats a successful 2025 while in a contract year. — Joseph Person
Yes, the breakout potential for the second-year tight end has that kind of ceiling . Loveland has a growing rapport with quarterback Caleb Williams, trust from play caller Ben Johnson and an expanding role that takes advantage of all his gifts. Even inside of a share-the-wealth Bears offense with impressive weaponry at all the skill positions, Loveland can sniff 90 catches, 1,000 yards and 10 touchdowns this season. His continued emergence will go a long way toward determining just how explosive the Bears offense can be. — Dan Wiederer
The ugly, horrific awfulness of the 2025 Bengals defense makes it hard to believe such a dramatic spike from 30th in points allowed to top 10 would be possible. But analyzing what the Bengals have on paper and showed during camp, particularly the energized dominance of Dexter Lawrence, it seems almost reasonable. Their defensive line flipped from fatal flaw to deep, disruptive chaos agent. Dropping Geno Stone for Bryan Cook at safety will do wonders for limiting explosive plays. They have stars, leadership, emerging young players and a boatload of confidence. Can defensive coordinator Al Golden bring the talent to life? Can the linebackers make Year 2 jumps with support in front of them? If yes, this could absolutely be a top-10 group. — Paul Dehner Jr.
The Browns have had at least three different starting quarterbacks in three straight seasons — and 12 times since the Browns returned to the NFL in 1999. The current streak seems likely to reach four as the Browns stubbornly give Deshaun Watson one more go in the final year of Watson’s albatross of a contract. Shedeur Sanders will be second up, but if Watson doesn’t make it out of September as the starter, the Browns could end up giving Dillon Gabriel or uber-athletic rookie Taylen Green a look late in the season. It’s not draft season yet, but it’s coming soon. — Zac Jackson
Gary’s career high is 9.5 sacks in 2021. He had 7.5 each of the last two seasons in Green Bay. He has looked like an extremely motivated player throughout training camp, getting as much pressure as any Dallas edge rusher. And the opportunities should be there with an interior defensive line that includes Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark. Gary and Donovan Ezeiruaku are the expected starters at outside linebacker. Von Miller and rookie Malachi Lawrence should see a lot of opportunities behind them. If Gary, 28, stays healthy, he has a chance to have a big year in Christian Parker’s new defensive scheme. — Jon Machota
This prediction can’t be considered a jinx for the oft-injured Dobbins. Not when the veteran himself offered “ a pinky promise ” at the start of training camp that he would play in all 17 regular-season games this season. Dobbins doesn’t need a perfect attendance record to reach the 1,000-yard milestone. He rushed for 772 yards in just 10 games in 2025 before suffering a Lisfranc injury that sidelined him for the rest of the season. So long as he can play 13 games, he’ll hit the 1,000-yard mark in a Denver offense committed to running the ball more this season. Perhaps more importantly, though, the Broncos appear prepared to withstand a potential absence from Dobbins thanks to the addition of rookie Jonah Coleman, who drew rave reviews from the coaching staff for his performance in camp. — Nick Kosmider
We’re talking bold, right? The last time we saw Alim McNeill at full strength, in 2024, he was playing at a Pro Bowl level. McNeill finished top 15 that season among qualified defensive tackles in pass-rush win rate and pressures before a torn ACL ended his season in December. McNeill returned in October 2025, but admitted he was overthinking on the field and regaining trust in his knee. It wasn’t the best version of himself. But now, McNeill believes he’s past the injury. Dan Campbell has raved about him, and offensive linemen say they can tell he’s looking himself again. If that’s the case, McNeill could finally be ready to reclaim his status as one of the league’s best young defensive tackles. — Colton Pouncy

To set the all-purpose mark (which includes return yards), he’ll need to top Darren Sproles’ 2,696 in 2011. This is not a bet that Robinson will return kicks for the Falcons this year. It’s a bet he’ll be overfed in both the rushing and passing scheme in Atlanta. — Josh Kendall
The arrival of Jesse Minter as head coach and Anthony Weaver as defensive coordinator has coincided with the return of swagger and confidence to a defense that fell on hard times last year. The addition of Trey Hendrickson and return of Nnamdi Madubuike has surely helped, too. Minter has brought in a defensive system that both attacks and deceives. The Ravens will need bounce-back years from Roquan Smith and Marlon Humphrey, but the mix of accomplished veterans and talented young players, plus a more attacking mindset, is a good recipe for the return of the ball-hawking Baltimore defense from the past. — Jeff Zrebiec
Walker was a fourth-round pick just a year ago, and those who have worked closely with him insist he’s on the verge of greatness . The gargantuan nose tackle slid down the 2025 draft chutes over a nagging back problem the University of Kentucky declined to shut down. So Walker soldiered forth, competing the best he could despite lost-cause game situations. Those performances hurt his stock. Buffalo weighed those reports before adding Walker and molding the rookie to become a star prospect who started every game except the opener. Walker is a 6-foot-7, 331-pound mauler, his oversized frame propelled by a relentless engine. Walker will see recurring opportunities to annihilate offensive lines and leave carriers in a heap. Those visuals will go a long way in establishing him as a bona fide baddie. — Tim Graham
The Panthers’ defense was the NFL’s worst in 2024, when Carolina gave up 404.5 yards and 31.4 points a game, and became the fourth team in NFL history to allow 3,000 rushing yards. Derrick Brown’s return helped the Panthers climb back to respectability last season (16th in total defense). And they look poised to take another jump this year, following the additions of edge rusher Jaelan Phillips and linebackers Devin Lloyd and Bobby Okereke. The interior D-line depth is a little lean, but the back end should be in good shape, provided Mike Jackson repeats a successful 2025 while in a contract year. — Joseph Person
Yes, the breakout potential for the second-year tight end has that kind of ceiling . Loveland has a growing rapport with quarterback Caleb Williams, trust from play caller Ben Johnson and an expanding role that takes advantage of all his gifts. Even inside of a share-the-wealth Bears offense with impressive weaponry at all the skill positions, Loveland can sniff 90 catches, 1,000 yards and 10 touchdowns this season. His continued emergence will go a long way toward determining just how explosive the Bears offense can be. — Dan Wiederer
The ugly, horrific awfulness of the 2025 Bengals defense makes it hard to believe such a dramatic spike from 30th in points allowed to top 10 would be possible. But analyzing what the Bengals have on paper and showed during camp, particularly the energized dominance of Dexter Lawrence, it seems almost reasonable. Their defensive line flipped from fatal flaw to deep, disruptive chaos agent. Dropping Geno Stone for Bryan Cook at safety will do wonders for limiting explosive plays. They have stars, leadership, emerging young players and a boatload of confidence. Can defensive coordinator Al Golden bring the talent to life? Can the linebackers make Year 2 jumps with support in front of them? If yes, this could absolutely be a top-10 group. — Paul Dehner Jr.
The Browns have had at least three different starting quarterbacks in three straight seasons — and 12 times since the Browns returned to the NFL in 1999. The current streak seems likely to reach four as the Browns stubbornly give Deshaun Watson one more go in the final year of Watson’s albatross of a contract. Shedeur Sanders will be second up, but if Watson doesn’t make it out of September as the starter, the Browns could end up giving Dillon Gabriel or uber-athletic rookie Taylen Green a look late in the season. It’s not draft season yet, but it’s coming soon. — Zac Jackson
Gary’s career high is 9.5 sacks in 2021. He had 7.5 each of the last two seasons in Green Bay. He has looked like an extremely motivated player throughout training camp, getting as much pressure as any Dallas edge rusher. And the opportunities should be there with an interior defensive line that includes Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark. Gary and Donovan Ezeiruaku are the expected starters at outside linebacker. Von Miller and rookie Malachi Lawrence should see a lot of opportunities behind them. If Gary, 28, stays healthy, he has a chance to have a big year in Christian Parker’s new defensive scheme. — Jon Machota
This prediction can’t be considered a jinx for the oft-injured Dobbins. Not when the veteran himself offered “ a pinky promise ” at the start of training camp that he would play in all 17 regular-season games this season. Dobbins doesn’t need a perfect attendance record to reach the 1,000-yard milestone. He rushed for 772 yards in just 10 games in 2025 before suffering a Lisfranc injury that sidelined him for the rest of the season. So long as he can play 13 games, he’ll hit the 1,000-yard mark in a Denver offense committed to running the ball more this season. Perhaps more importantly, though, the Broncos appear prepared to withstand a potential absence from Dobbins thanks to the addition of rookie Jonah Coleman, who drew rave reviews from the coaching staff for his performance in camp. — Nick Kosmider
We’re talking bold, right? The last time we saw Alim McNeill at full strength, in 2024, he was playing at a Pro Bowl level. McNeill finished top 15 that season among qualified defensive tackles in pass-rush win rate and pressures before a torn ACL ended his season in December. McNeill returned in October 2025, but admitted he was overthinking on the field and regaining trust in his knee. It wasn’t the best version of himself. But now, McNeill believes he’s past the injury. Dan Campbell has raved about him, and offensive linemen say they can tell he’s looking himself again. If that’s the case, McNeill could finally be ready to reclaim his status as one of the league’s best young defensive tackles. — Colton Pouncy
The Packers’ 2025 first-round pick caught just 29 passes for 361 yards last year. He didn’t score a touchdown in the regular season. Golden battled injuries, but his rookie year fell well short of everyone’s expectations anyway. That wasn’t for a lack of…

title: Eagles superlatives: Jalen Carter for DPOY? Jalyx Hunt, Jihaad Campbell poised to break out From Jalen Carter’s DPOY chances to potential breakout stars, our Eagles superlatives offer predictions for the 2026 season. Zach Berman 3
summary:
Philadelphia Eagles DT Jalen Carter could contend for Defensive Player of the Year if he turns his disruptive play into bigger sack totals. Mitchell Leff / Getty Images
Week 1 is here. All those training camp practice reports are last month’s news. The preseason hype and debates will be forgotten in Philadelphia come Sunday at 4:25 p.m. ET, when the Eagles kick off against the Washington Commanders.
There’s no use in writing, “I told you so!” four months from now, so let’s document superlatives
full_text:
Philadelphia Eagles DT Jalen Carter could contend for Defensive Player of the Year if he turns his disruptive play into bigger sack totals. Mitchell Leff / Getty Images
Week 1 is here. All those training camp practice reports are last month’s news. The preseason hype and debates will be forgotten in Philadelphia come Sunday at 4:25 p.m. ET, when the Eagles kick off against the Washington Commanders.
There’s no use in writing, “I told you so!” four months from now, so let’s document superlatives before the storylines shuffle. ( Here’s the 2025 version for comparison’s sake. )
Jalen Carter as Defensive Player of the Year
The Eagles might have the NFL’s best defense this season, and Carter could be their best player. He signed a deal making him the highest-paid defensive tackle in the NFL . He enters this season healthier than last year. Remember how he looked in the postseason in January 2025? Carter can have that effect all year. His statistics have not matched his impact on games in his career (13.5 sacks in three seasons), though it wouldn’t be far-fetched to see that sack number increase. It would be difficult for a defensive tackle to win the award without double-digit sacks.
Carter’s preseason odds have been in the top 10 in this category by multiple sportsbooks. Jalen Hurts as MVP was under consideration, although I’m not sure he’ll accumulate prolific passing numbers even if the Eagles are among the NFL’s best teams. Carter leading the NFL’s No. 1 defense might be a better path to an award.
Last year: Jalen Hurts as MVP
Without A.J. Brown, Smith is in line for a major jump in volume and production. Even if the Eagles are a run-first team, that type of increase could put Smith firmly in contention with the top four receivers in the NFC.
Smith has averaged 121.4 targets per 17 games during the past four seasons; Brown averaged 142.9 per 17 games. If Smith remains healthy and is targeted 150 times, he could finish with 90-100 catches and 1,250-1,500 yards. If he’s targeted 160-plus times like Puka Nacua and Jaxon Smith-Njigba, watch out. Jordan Mailata also remains a perennial contender for this award. Jordan Davis might have a word, too.
If last season was a “breakout” year for Hunt by leading the Eagles in sacks and interceptions, this season might be the year he’s recognized as one of the NFL’s top young edge rushers. Double-digit sacks are within reach. He was one of the best players on the field this summer. He has the tools to do everything desired at the position, and his skills match his frame and athleticism. Hunt could follow Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean by leaping to stardom. Sharing snaps with Jonathan Greenard and Nolan Smith might help: 5.5 of Hunt’s 6.5 sacks last season came after the Eagles acquired Jaelan Phillips, including two multi-sack performances.
Last year: Quinyon Mitchell
Campbell is stepping into an important role, replacing Nakobe Dean. There’s a reason the Eagles drafted Campbell in the first round and let Dean leave in free agency. He has the talent to be a difference-making off-ball linebacker, with a rare combination of length and speed at the position. It’s his second year in Vic Fangio’s scheme. He missed time this offseason and had an up-and-down camp, but he’s playing next to Zack Baun and behind one of the best lines in football. Look for Campbell to take a jump, similar to Moro Ojomo last season. Dontayvion Wicks is also in contention for this category.
When he’s healthy, Dickerson is among the NFL’s best guards. It’s helpful that he’s not coming off surgery this season, but there’s considerable wear and tear on his body. The Eagles were already managing his workload this summer. He’s hailed for his toughness, and appropriately so, but Dickerson admitted he shouldn’t keep playing through injuries.
Dickerson shot down offseason retirement rumors. He restructured his contract, and he’s past the guaranteed money on his deal. If he can stay healthy, there might not be a step back. But what toll have the injuries taken on him?
For one of the NFL’s biggest stars and a focal point of the offense, the hype around Barkley has been too quiet this summer. He’s not coming off an Offensive Player of the Year award and a 2,000-yard campaign like last season. So much attention goes to Hurts’ adjustment to the new offense and the new receiver corps. It’s easy to forget that this is likely going to be a run-first offense and their best chance to win big is having Barkley contend again for the NFL rushing crown.
It’s certainly possible — his enthusiasm for the new scheme and a healthier offensive line give him a chance to bounce back. Barkley is competitive and likely will want to push back on any idea that he’s declining at age 29. His over/under for rushing yards is 1,099 yards. Take the over, as long as he stays healthy.
This was a race between the top reserve offensive tackle and the top reserve interior offensive lineman, so I’ll lean toward the interior because of the way Kendall played this summer and his ability to help in multiple spots. His development impressed the Eagles this offseason. Howie Roseman had questions about the interior offensive line depth in camp. Kendall (and Willie Lampkin) answered them. Markel Bell is a candidate here. So is Tank Bigsby, who would need to step into a large role if Barkley goes down.
Dallas Goedert is a key offensive player with a notable injury history, and the depth behind him remains a major question mark. Johnny Mundt is more of a blocker at this stage of his career. Eli Stowers, the second-round pick, had a slow camp and might be a better bet for a 2027 impact. The Eagles like E.J. Jenkins more than the public, and Grant Calcaterra is a candidate to be activated off IR. Do any of these options give you confidence if Goedert goes down? He played 15 games last season for the first time since 2021. Even if Goedert is healthy, a complementary tight end who can help in the passing game would be a sensible upgrade. I expect Roseman will scan his options.
There’s been much conversation about a future Hurts contract decision. What about Barkley, one of the franchise’s most high-profile players? He’s guaranteed $2.5 million of his option bonus next season — down from the guaranteed $16.75 million this year, including his base salary — and 2027 is his age-30 season. Barkley is an outlier and could remain one of the NFL’s top rushers into his 30s. The Eagles would need to absorb a big cap hit if they moved on from him after this season, so the contract could remain the status quo.
He’s in a similar situation to Christian McCaffrey; Barkley and McCaffrey are Nos. 4 and 5 in running back salaries, respectively, after other backs received new deals. The quarterback always receives more headlines, but I’m curious if the Eagles have a decision to make on Barkley, too.
Last year: What’s Nakobe Dean’s role?
The Eagles’ reconfigured wide receiver depth chart was hard to ascertain this summer with DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon missing three weeks of team drills. They need to avoid this looking like 2021, the season before A.J. Brown’s arrival. Smith showed clear upside that year, except the help around him kept the passing offense from reaching the level it needed.
There’s a chance this all works as designed, with Smith looking like the bona fide No. 1 receiver, Wicks taking a leap with more opportunity in a familiar offense and Lemon showcasing the type of dynamic run-after-catch ability that made him such a threat at USC. Hollywood Brown and Elijah Moore offer experienced depth while Darius Cooper continues the development curve on display this summer. That’s the ideal scenario.
Replacing Brown’s production in the aggregate makes sense on paper. It’s still possible they miss Brown more than fans might realize — and this looks like the season that compelled the Eagles to acquire Brown in the first place.
Last year: No. 2 cornerback

summary:

MELBOURNE, Australia — Where are the Los Angeles Rams?
That’s been the big question this week from locals around town, as would-be NFL fans get ready for the first game in Australia. The San Francisco 49ers arrived here Friday morning and have made an appearance at an Australian Football League game
full_text:
The 49ers arrived Friday and have made several appearances around Melbourne before settling in for practice at AAMI Park ahead of this week's game against the Rams. Martin Keep / AFP via Getty Images
MELBOURNE, Australia — Where are the Los Angeles Rams?
That’s been the big question this week from locals around town, as would-be NFL fans get ready for the first game in Australia. The San Francisco 49ers arrived here Friday morning and have made an appearance at an Australian Football League game, held a clinic for Special Olympics athletes and even had a workshop for fans to learn key phrases for cheers at Thursday’s game. It will be Friday in Australia when it’s played.
It’s hard to get around town without seeing a 49ers billboard or jersey.
Sun came out for a walk around Melbourne. No one has heard of the Rams. #49ers pic.twitter.com/cQoc10RWXg
— Vic Tafur (@VicTafur) September 6, 2026
Niners coach Kyle Shanahan, for other reasons, was surprised by the city of Melbourne.
“I don’t see kangaroos and crocodiles everywhere,” Shanahan said before Monday’s practice at AAMI Park. “I was expecting to see that. It looks like a very normal, cool city.”
The Rams will have to take his word for it, as they don’t arrive until Thursday. The home team — an ironic twist — has the opposite travel strategy as the 49ers: They are attempting to play in the game without changing their body clocks, and the 49ers are building in a week to shake off whatever jet lag players might have.
The two approaches will be long debated. The Rams seem to be more concerned with the aftereffects from this trip and don’t want to have to reset their body clocks twice before traveling to New York to face the Giants in Week 2, followed by a tough home game against the Denver Broncos.
The 49ers, on the other hand, are not as worried about the back end, with home games against two of the worst teams in the league in weeks 2 and 3, the Miami Dolphins and Arizona Cardinals.
But one question that has emerged in the last few days is what effect those approaches will have on the crowd Friday. With the 49ers taking time to embrace their hosts — their cheerleaders helped young locals set a world record Sunday for largest cheerleading dance (1,424 people) — it’s interesting to ponder whether they will have louder fans in the stands now.
That would be another twist. The Rams, as you remember, requested the 49ers as their opponent for this game because they were wary of all the 49ers fans who took over their stadium when the teams played at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles.
“It was disappointing to let them off the hook and get them out of that,” said Shanahan, who hated the idea of this game when it was first announced. “But, I have a feeling knowing how our fans roll … I have a feeling they won’t be much different here. I expect to have a good showing. … After being here for a couple days, this is the right time to be here, it’s the right place to be, and it’s the right team to go against.”

title: 6 Cardinals Position Battles — Every Winner Before Week 1
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals' regular season is here.
The Cardinals' entire offseason is officially behind them — we've made it to game week, where the Los Angeles Chargers play host at SoFi Stadium this coming Sunday.
Arizona's roster evaluation is officially over. The Cardinals now have roles defined and move into the work week as such with head coach Mike LaFleur having his team set .
Months ago, we entered OTAs with plenty of roster spots and position battles up for grabs. Here's who won every single one:
James Conner hit injured reserve, so this was effectively RB3 behind Jeremiyah Love and Tyler Allgeier. Bam Knight and Trey Benson were considered to be battling here, though thanks to Benson's injury and Knight's impressive preseason, this was anything but a battle. Knight safely had a roster spot while Benson was waived/injured before the preseason even ended.
The Cardinals' top of the WR room felt fairly comfortable with five spots cemented — but who would emerge strong enough to convince Arizona to keep a sixth? As fate would have it, Jalen Brooks and Simi Fehoko played so well to force the Cardinals to keep seven receivers. Ihmir Smith-Marsette was the initial leader here before he fell out of favor.
Second-round pick Chase Bisontis was set to make this quite the conversation, especially with impressive play in preseason before going down with his MCL injury. Still, with legal issues pending, Adams was the slight favorite to begin the season as a starter. Now, barring a surprise from Jon Gaines, Adams has a clear path to starting for the rest of the season.
There's no clear winner here, because the Cardinals will deploy both Gibbens and Simon differently week to week based on matchups, gameplans, etc.
Gibbens most likely will be used as nickel linebacker thanks to his frame and pass coverage abilities. Simon, meanwhile, better fits a run-stopping/early down package.
The spot opposite of Mack Wilson Sr. appears to be an open door for both Cardinals linebackers to get plenty of run and playing time — at least until somebody can truly separate themselves.
Garrett Williams is back in the slot. Will Johnson obviously carries starting duties on one boundary spot — but what about the other?
Burke, a Day 3 rookie who shined last season, has a strong grasp on starting duties to begin his second season after nobody else in the Cardinals' cornerback room really proved themselves in preseason. Kei'Trel Clark and Max Melton sit as potential alternates here.
This may have been one of the more surprising jobs of camp/preseason, as we all assumed Dadrion Taylor-Demerson would step into the departing Jalen Thompson's shoes and start next to Budda Baker.
Andrew Wingard flipped that script.
Wingard, who signed as a free agent, took an early lead in the safety room next to Baker and hasn't looked back. He's firmly entrenched as a starter entering Week 1 while Taylor-Demerson hasn't been able to impress.

title: Cardinals Mailbag: Jeremiyah Love's Recovery, Josh Sweat Trade Talk and Arizona's Biggest Question Marks
full_text:
The regular season is upon us.
At this time next week, the Arizona Cardinals will be in Los Angeles to compete with the Chargers in their regular season opener.
To everybody: Congrats, we've made it. Football season is here.
And thanks to everybody for your questions for today's mailbag. Really hoping all of your seasons (real and fantasy) go in your favor.
Eric, Jayden Williams had a meteoric rise through training camp, and perhaps he shouldn't have slid to the seventh round in the draft — though this is very much Elijah Wilkinson's job to lose.
It's fair to say Wilkinson is "dead set" as the starter to begin the season, and for what it's worth, Arizona really likes their new right tackle. He fits for what the team wants to do in terms of zone usage in the run game.
With that established, Wilkinson has been hit and miss through the course of his career — Cardinals fans are aware of this. It wouldn't surprise me to see Wilkinson usurped at some point this season, though Arizona would probably play Josh Fryar ahead of Williams if that was the case.
Frankie, if the team is healthy, Arizona should at very bare minimum surpass that three-win total from last season. 2025 was truly a season to forget where practically everything that could go wrong, did.
With that said, Nick Rallis is on a short leash. The Cardinals' defense simply has to perform better. How much will that unit look differently with Jonathan Gannon now out of the picture? That's one of the biggest questions in the desert, one that could sway the pendulum in either direction.
I'd say true, to answer your question. Nearly 70% of NFL games come down to one possession, and with Mike LaFleur running the show, there should no doubt be a few games the Cardinals should flip that previously would have gone out of their favor.
That leads into our next question:
The Cardinals' defense is what will truly sway 2026. That's not groundbreaking, though it's impossible to really overstate how crucial that side of the ball will be.
If we get a repeat of last season, we'll see similar results. The Cardinals' offense should be a fun watch, though if they're forced into a track meet every week, that's not sustainable for success.
Arizona didn't really upgrade their unit this offseason, rather filling gaps left by departing players. With most of the same cast, and the same coordinator, it's reasonable to have some pessimism surrounding the defense.
On a scale 1-10, probably a 6. Ask me again in a few weeks and that could change drastically.
That's a great question, Mando.
For strongest position, it sure feels like the receiver room, right? The Cardinals were so impressed with that group, seven players were kept at the position. It's strong from 1-7 with everybody offering a little something different for the roster.
As for the weakest, my eyes jumped straight to outside linebacker. Josh Sweat's presence carries an incredible amount of weight for a room that failed to produce much of anything last year. The Cardinals opted to plug other spots, and as a result their pass rush will likely resemble last year's — which isn't a good thing.
Ed, that's a tough cookie to crumble.
Chargers. Seahawks. 49ers. Only Seattle is at home. That's a massive challenge for a team that moved on from both their franchise quarterback and head coach in the same offseason.
The good news here? Arizona could have a bit of early season unpredictability in LaFleur's offense. Less tape for teams to evaluate generates a larger gap of gray area, one that plays into Arizona's favor.
Tough? Sure. But it wouldn't be in the least surprising to see the Cardinals steal one of these games.
Taking a quick scan at the schedule, the Bills have to play the Texans, Lions and Chargers. That's not ideal either.
Colin, Love truly does feel like he's a 50/50 shot to play in this game.
The good news is he's moving around quite well in the clips people are posting of him online. No restrictive brace and him being barefoot recovery signals he's getting closer.
However, it's a long season — and Arizona will want to be diligent with their first-round pick.
My unofficial prediction is Love will play but Tyler Allgeier mostly handles duties as the Cardinals ease Love back into the mix.
Thanks for the question, Jacob.
I feel like it would be easy to give you the big names, but sometimes Kendrick Bourne's performance was overshadowed. Cardinals fans have already warmed up to him thanks to his energy, though he legitimately had a solid outing in training camp — catching everything sent his way.
Defensively, Eku Leota really had a nice outing. We previously discussed Arizona's lack of production at outside linebacker, though perhaps there's a hidden gem in Leota, who seemed to always be in the Cardinals' backfield.
Jayden, NFL rules state that barring relocation or change of ownership, teams must wait at least five years to change their uniforms.
The Cardinals unveiled their most recent set for the 2023 season, marking at minimum two more years before Arizona can make the change again.
Will they? Plenty of people want them to. The uniforms were a step in the right direction after a much needed change, though there's clearly still a ways to go.
I really appreciate all of the questions you sent, but thought I would specifically answer this one.
Things I do believe: Josh Sweat requested a trade after the Cardinals fired Jonathan Gannon.
Things I do not believe: Arizona would go all offseason knowing their star pass rusher was unhappy and would trade him right before the start of the season.
I think Sweat to the Packers, in a vacuum, makes sense. I also think it's entirely possible he's traded further down the line.
But Arizona wasn't trading Sweat now. Him being activated the week of their preseason finale in Green Bay was simply the Cardinals waiting until the last minute to avoid him landing on reserve and missing the first four games of the season.
It was quite hilarious to hear some of the chatter/buzz emerging from that side of the country last week. Those same people who pushed hard for Sweat-to-Green Bay chatter backpedaled like prime Deion Sanders.
Maybe the power of manifestation is just that strong in Packer country.

title: 3 Cardinals Lineup Decisions I'd Make If I Were Mike LaFleur in Week 1
full_text:
We're one week out from the Arizona Cardinals beginning their regular season slate, and the time to make some crucial roster decisions for Week 1 is rapidly approaching.
The Cardinals likely have a good idea of what their lineup and rotation will look like against the Los Angeles Chargers to start the season. There's some tough calls — but here's what I would do if I were head coach Mike LaFleur :
Jeremiyah Love exited his only preseason action with a high ankle sprain, and reports indicate he's a true 50/50 toss-up for Week 1. Love will have just a couple days shy of a full month to recover before SoFi Stadium awaits.
Love is a supremely talented player that fans (and the Cardinals) want to see as much as possible. That's understandable. However, tossing Love back into the mix with a heavy workload isn't the wisest of moves.
That's with the Cardinals having a strong alternative in Tyler Allgeier/Bam Knight and an offense under LaFleur that should be balanced in its approach.
The season is not won or lost in one week — especially a season opener. If Love does play, he should be on a snap count to help his transition back to the playing field.
One of few Cardinals position battles that ensued over the summer appeared at inside linebacker, where Jack Gibbens and Cody Simon competed for the second inside linebacker job next to Mack Wilson Sr.
Simon had an early grasp on the job — taking majority of first-team reps — before Gibbens made a strong push towards the end of preseason.
It's likely the Cardinals will deploy both depending on the down and distance, though Gibbens' profile as an athletic body who can defend the pass would give Arizona a better option against a quarterback such as Justin Herbert, who has the arm to make any throw across the field.
Simon should be involved in obvious run situations — though Gibbens projects as the better fit next to Wilson.
Robinson carries first-round pedigree but has yet to produce to those expectations.
Time is running out for Robinson's window to be a starter for this Cardinals defense. Arizona loves what they've seen out of Walter Nolen while the combo of Roy Lopez and Andrew Billings as run-stuffers should bode well in the trenches.
Truth be told, the Cardinals deploy practically everybody in the DL room on game days, so the "starter" label really doesn't mean much. That said, Arizona should undoubtedly hand more snaps to Dante Stills over Robinson.
Stills isn't talked about enough — he's consistent, but not flashy. Stills raises the floor of Arizona's defensive line room and could perhaps produce more if allowed. On the other side of the coin, Robinson truly needs to prove himself entering a pivotal third season.
Robinson should and will still get significant snaps. However, making the former top pick earn starting duties isn't such a bad idea here.

title: Michael Wilson's Cardinals Extension: Full Contract Breakdown — And Arizona's Easy Out
full_text:
Details of Michael Wilson's contract extension with the Arizona Cardinals have been revealed, and as expected, there's some fairly team friendly aspects towards the end of the deal.
The Cardinals re-worked Wilson's 2026 cap structure alongside handing him a three-year extension that ensures Wilson is under contract in Arizona through 2029. The new deal is worth $75 million and carries an annual average of $25 million. $35 million was fully guaranteed at signing.
Most notably, Wilson has his salaries in 2026 and 2027 fully guaranteed. Wilson also secured a $18 million signing bonus and $12 million of his 2028 salary is injury guaranteed.
However, if Arizona wants to get out of the deal in the future, it's fairly easy. The Cardinals can save $13.6 million in the 2028 offseason and $24.9 million in the 2029 offseason with pre-June 1 cuts of Wilson, if they feel necessary.

Base salary: $21,814,000 Prorated signing bonus: $4,500,000 Regular roster bonus: $2,500,000 Per game roster bonus : $340,000 Workout bonus: $250,000 Guaranteed salary: $0 Cap number: $29,404,000
Wilson is one of the hardest-working players in the locker room, so to see him rewarded was heartwarming for Cardinals coaches and players alike.
"There's no one more deserving than him," fellow Cardinals WR Simi Fehoko said.
Head coach Mike LaFleur added , "It's awesome. It's great for the Cardinals. It's great for his teammates, this locker room. It's good for our fan base. If anyone that really knows Mike, you can't help but root for the guy."
Wilson joins Hjalte Froholdt as recent Cardinals players to receive extensions this summer while slotting alongside previous big names in Budda Baker, James Conner and Trey McBride to receive sizable paydays under GM Monti Ossenfort.

title: Where Every Cardinals Roster Cut Landed
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals' initial 53-man roster is set.
The Cardinals parted ways with nearly 40 players this past weekend ahead of the regular season. Arizona didn't claim anybody on waivers, signaling confidence in their current corps of guys.
Still, a handful of Cardinals hit the open market — where have they landed?
Murphy-Bunting was one of the more surprising releases, as the veteran cornerback restructured his contract to remain with the Cardinals this past offseason. He held the most experience in Arizona's cornerback room and had moved to the slot to cover for Garrett Williams while he recovered from injury.
Williams came back faster than anticipated, pushing Murphy-Bunting down the depth chart and eventually lost out to other younger names.
Late-round pick Karson Sharar ultimately won the job over Pappoe, though the inside linebacker still has plenty to offer elsewhere. Pappoe, despite possessing a massive amount of speed, special teams prowess and three years of experience under his belt, simply was buried in Arizona's inside linebacker room.
Whether that changes in Tennessee remains to be seen, though a change of scenery should be good for Pappoe.
The Packers sure love them some Cardinals quarterbacks! Slovis is next in line after Green Bay added Clayton Tune following roster cuts last season. Slovis seemed doomed to be cut after Arizona added Gardner Minshew and Carson Beck this offseason.
As it turns out, Arizona's preseason finale against the Packers was a successful tryout for Slovis.

title: Cardinals Send a Message to the Locker Room with Michael Wilson Extension
full_text:
ARIZONA — The ink on Arizona Cardinals WR Michael Wilson's contract extension is dry, and across the board, it was a massive win.
Wilson secured a three-year extension with an annual salary of $25 million. The deal can be worth up to $78 million in total with $47 million guaranteed.
"It's awesome. It's great for the Cardinals. It's great for his teammates, this locker room. It's good for our fan base. If anyone that really knows Mike, you can't help but root for the guy," Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur said after the deal got done.
Wilson did well in a contact extension that saw him usurp recent receiver deals in Michael Pittman Jr. and Christian Watson this offseason. However, it wasn't just Wilson that emerges with positive light.
The Cardinals faced plenty of criticism this offseason for failing to reach extensions with Wilson and fellow 2023 draft pick Paris Johnson Jr.
Arizona did seal an extension with Hjalte Froholdt, though that was minor in comparison to the money Wilson and Johnson were pursuing.
Yet a deal did get done. And though it won't be without its doubters regardless of the overall money awarded, it was big for not only Cardinals GM Monti Ossenfort — but also a locker room that now knows their general manager will reward their hard work.
"I think you'd have to ask the players that. But from my perspective, I think this shows them that we're trying to keep really good players that are really good for the locker room, that are going to help us — in this case on offense move the ball forward and cross into the end zone," LaFleur added.
"And so I love our guys' mind is, even if this didn't get done. But I think naturally in any locker room when you sign something like that, those guys are going to be happy for one the Arizona Cardinals and two, for the human."
Drafting and developing has been a massive calling card for the Cardinals since Ossenfort took over in 2023. This offseason was the first opportunity for Ossenfort's regime to begin extensions of his own draft picks, and while there's still plenty of work ahead — Wilson's deal meant a lot more than just to the player:
"It's awesome because, like you said, you drafted them. You put a lot of time into that process, and they get here, then you're working on developing the person and the player," LaFleur added.
"You have one of those guys in this situation get signed to the deal he did — It's a big deal."

title: How Cardinals Preseason Underdog Eku Leota Survived Roster Cuts
full_text:
ARIZONA — There's a whole lot of gratitude when it comes to Arizona Cardinals linebacker Eku Leota.
Leota was one of Arizona's surprise camp and preseason standouts after signing with the team's practice squad last December. Often times, players like Leota are simply bodies to help fill out a 90-man preseason roster.
Yet Leota made play — after play – after play, making so much noise in both practice and games that the Cardinals couldn't leave him off their roster.
"Man, a lot of just feeling grateful, and that hard work really does pay off at the end of the day. Just to have the right people here in my corner: teammates, coaches pushing me every day. I know it's a competition, but the person I was competing with the most was myself every day, and that's how I looked at it throughout the whole training camp," said Leota.
"It's just me being better every day and peaking at the right time, which is right now."
The Cardinals ultimately parted ways with former second-round pick BJ Ojulari in the outside linebackers room, a bit of a surprising decision. Ojulari himself wasn't the best version of himself, though Leota undoubtedly earned a spot.
"This is my fourth team. I've been in four different schemes, and just being able to take everything that I learned from other teams, but trying to put it in the right areas within this game," said Leota.
"I feel like they let me play free from a schematic standpoint here, and being able to play within the scheme, but with my skill set as well. So, Just being able to get off the ball, and then using a lot of speed, and converting that speed into power."
Often times, players on the practice squad aren't viewed in the same light as those on the active 53-man roster. Leota says his prior experience was massive in helping him earn time on task to go out and do what he did this preseason — get after the quarterback.
"Oh, it helped out a lot. I know I was a P [practice] squad last year, but just being a scout team player, and I'm sure I'm going to be a scout team player again this year, which I need those reps. I like going against the ones, and those are my game reps throughout the week because I'm not going to get a lot of game reps, so I try to get my game reps in throughout the week," he said.
"Special teams though is where I'm gonna get my reps. So that's where I take pride in special teams."
For a player such as Leota, special teams is mandatory if he'll survive on the roster. However, his abilities as an outside linebacker could still impact a Cardinals room needing some sort of breakout at the spot opposite of Josh Sweat.
"Coach Nick [Rallis] our DC, he believes in my ability, and he told me to go play free, and I did. So I'm grateful for him, and to have a coach to believe in you, it helps a lot," Leota said.

title: Michael Wilson Got His Payday — But He Wants a Cardinals Turnaround Even More
full_text:
ARIZONA — Today felt like a massive win for the Arizona Cardinals, their fans, and Michael Wilson all in one swoop.
The ink is still drying on Wilson's contract extension with the organization, to the tune of a three-year deal worth $25 million annually. Reports indicate the contract can be worth up to $78 million total with incentives.
Wilson got paid, leaping the likes of Christian Watson and Michael Pittman Jr. this offseason after both signed their respective deals. The Cardinals keep what they hope to be a core piece of their team for the foreseeable future, and fans finally see a drafted and developed talent under general manager Monti Ossenfort sign an extension.
The Cardinals haven't won the division in over a decade. They also haven't been in a playoff game since 2021. There's been glimpses of hope they could turn things around, but nothing more than a flash in the pan.
That could potentially change under new head coach Mike LaFleur, who has spoke so glowingly of Wilson and what he could potentially be in the offense.
Wilson could have opted to chase more money or find a new team after this season. However, he stuck around — and he wants to be part of the reason the Cardinals turn things around.
"I love the organization. I love living in the state of Arizona. I love the people in Arizona, and I think when you can be a centerpiece and flip something, that's way more gratifying and rewarding," Wilson said when asked why he re-signed with the Cardinals.
"Going through the dark days, the tough times, when you've lost bad games, when there's more Niner fans than Arizona fans. Like, how cool would that be this season when the stadium's packed and we're in a race for the playoffs or a playoff team and we're in the playoffs? Being a centerpiece of changing, like turning the tides. I think that sense of loyalty — that just screams the type of player and person that I want to be.
"I want to be a centerpiece to a franchise and be a guy that was a cornerstone piece that helped flip it. What better place to do it in Arizona? I keep saying it, but I got so much love for Arizona. I genuinely do, and not even tied to the franchise — I can see myself living here for the rest of my life. So I want to bring good vibes, wins to the fan base and to the organization.
"I definitely feel a sense of debt, and I'm gonna work my hardest every single day to show why I deserve that deal."

title: Michael Wilson Admits He Wasn't Sure Cardinals Contract Would Get Done
full_text:
ARIZONA — Even Michael Wilson was swept up in contract rumors before putting pen to paper .
24 hours ago, the Arizona Cardinals' receiver didn't know if an extension was going to be reached before the start of the regular season. With today being the final day of practice before the team parts for the weekend, there was an unofficial but hopeful deadline for Wilson and the Cardinals to strike a deal.
Wilson and Arizona indeed found a middle ground, reaching an agreement on a three-year, $75 million deal that can be worth up to $78 million — $47 million was guaranteed.
However, Wilson himself admitted to reporters he wasn't so sure something would get done.
"Talks have been going on since early offseason, and so I definitely wanted to get the deal done prior to Week 1, just for obvious reasons. And one, I wanted to know that I had security being in Arizona, but I think everyone saw the report yesterday," Wilson said near the beginning of his press conference.
The report came from ESPN's Dan Graziano, who suggested the Cardinals and Wilson were so far off that numerous sources told him Wilson was likely to hit free agency.
Yet the tide turned quickly to ensure Wilson wouldn't hit the open market next offseason.
"Things, conversations happened, tides turned, and the deal happened to get done. I couldn't even sleep last night, I was just so excited. I'm just so excited it got done."
Wilson also said contract talks were long and the two sides sometimes went weeks without communication.
"They were long. I'm not going to say I was nervous about it not getting done, but there were times where both sides, we didn't speak for a couple weeks and kind of reevaluating things," Wilson added.
"But I try to stay out of it as much as possible and let my agent handle it because — I said this early in offseason — like I didn't want to let a contract dictate how I played, performed, and the way that I showed up for my coaches and teammates throughout the offseason.
"So I tried my best to stay out of it and not bring it onto the field, not bring it into the locker room, and let Monti [Ossenfort] and his team handle it, my team handle it."
The Cardinals and Wilson both ultimately emerge as winners — Arizona retains arguably their top receiver at the moment while Wilson gets an annual contract value of $25 million per season.
And sometimes, that winning shot comes at the buzzer.

title: Falcons Officially Name Their Week 1 Starting Quarterback
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH – After a summer competition, the Atlanta Falcons have officially named Tua Tagovailoa the starting quarterback for Week 1. The Falcons confirmed the decision on Monday, six days before the Falcons travel to Pittsburgh to take on the Steelers.
Tua Tagovailoa has been named starting quarterback for Week 1 https://t.co/67barjCycW pic.twitter.com/l9QwpkUZOA
Tagovailoa beat out Michael Penix Jr. for the role for the time being, but the two’s competition only really got underway two weeks ago after the latter was cleared for full team drills. Penix, who tore his ACL in Week 11, did not participate in the preseason even though he was cleared ahead of the Falcons’ final matchup with the Dolphins.
In his place, Tagovailoa took the first-team reps, but was largely unimpressive . After a poor performance against the Broncos, he went 7-of-8 for 95 yards against his former team. Tagovailoa led a touchdown drive to start the game, but also lost a fumble after a botched snap with backup center Corey Levin.
The fumble was his second of the preseason, and it became a concern over the course of the summer, with Tagovailoa dropping a ball during practice at Lanier High School and losing another during the joint-practice sessions with the Colts.
The Falcons signed Tagovailoa earlier this offseason on a one-year, $1.2 million deal after he spent the last six seasons. Over an up-and-down career, the veteran has led the NFL in passer rating (2022), passing yards (2023), and completion percentage (2024). Last season, he was released for an NFL-record $99.2 million in dead money after throwing 15 interceptions and struggling with more injuries.
Penix, meanwhile, has been a part-time participant for the Falcons during training camp. He only participated in 7-on-7 drills, while Tagovailoa took the majority of team drills. The incumbent starter has started just 12 games over his two professional seasons, accruing a 4-8 overall record while completing 59.6% of his passes for 2,757 yards, 12 touchdowns, and six interceptions.
Despite the decision, there is still a reasonable chance that both Penix and Tagovailoa will start games for the Falcons this season.
With the continued uncertainty at quarterback, general manager Ian Cunningham opted to carry four quarterbacks on the roster . Cooper Rush and rookie undrafted free agent Jack Strand join Tagovailoa and Penix on the 53-man roster. Those two will occupy depth roles for the Falcons this season after they enjoyed strong preseason performances, aside from Rush’s first-week struggles.
With the starter decision now official, the Falcons will continue their preparations for the Steelers in Week 1 on Sunday. Kickoff is scheduled for 1:00 in Pittsburgh.

title: Why the Falcons Kept Four Quarterbacks on Their 53-Man Roster
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH – The Atlanta Falcons are the only team in the NFL that has not yet named a starting quarterback, but they were one of four teams to carry four of them on their active roster.
As the competition raged at Falcons headquarters for both the starting and third-string jobs, first-year general manager Ian Cunningham chose to retain all the competitors as the evaluation continues. Kevin Stefanski will announce the Week 1 starter, which will likely be either Michael Penix Jr. or Tua Tagovailoa, but veteran Cooper Rush and the upstart undrafted free agent Jack Strand made late pushes.
“The more reps, the more evaluations we can get, the better, right,” Falcons general manager Cunningham said. “Just like we discussed, that's the hand that we were dealt with. So, the more opportunities that we can get to evaluate, the better it is.”
All four players had legitimate arguments for retention.
Penix only has two weeks of practice with full team participation. Tagovailoa easily has the most starting experience in the NFL. Rush is a veteran backup. Strand opened eyes this summer with some outstanding preseason performances, and while he is not considered a likely option to start anytime soon, there was a good chance he would not last on the practice squad.
Not all four players will have a role on the field this season, but each provides a level of insurance that the Falcons critically need.
“If you let a guy like Cooper go, there’s a potential that he may be able to get an opportunity to go to another team. If you let a guy like Jack Strand go, he’s subject to waivers. And the way he played, [makes that risky],” Cunningham explained. “We talk about all the time draft, develop, retain – in his (Strand) case, he was undrafted, but to develop. There's a chance that somebody could have claimed him. I think it's about living in the now but also living in the future with Jack. So that kind of went into the four-quarterback thought process.”
The decision makes sense, but it carries repercussions down the line. As a result of this decision – or really indecision – the Falcons were forced to part ways with several players who would have had more significant roles on the team come Week 1.
They carried just two running backs, cut several veteran edge rushers , and had no room for rotational defensive linemen like Zach Harrison.
“I feel like that's a little bit of the roster gymnastics,” Cunningham said about his decision to retain the four players and how it impacts the rest of the roster. “You have to sacrifice some at some position but also know that we've got 16 practice squad spots. So, being thoughtful in that too, of who you put on practice squad, where you have certain spots, where we feel comfortable about some elevations if we need that.
“I think that's where you've got to get a little bit creative and feel like we're in that space right now. And it will probably change throughout the season. Just because we start with this 53 now, it may not be the same 53 that it is Week 18.”
The roster is far from settled, but not much else can happen until the Falcons make their QB1 decision – that is expected to come on Monday. That decision could trigger another round of roster moves as Cunningham continues balancing what Atlanta needs now with what it hopes to build for later.
